column2: the shaft strike's crush pressure, 84.1 MPa, is the card's reduction of a Janka side hardness: 8,400 N (FPL-GTR-282 Table 5-3a, shagbark, 12 % moisture) over the 99.9 mm2 projected area of an 11.28 mm ball embedded 5.64 mm. The strike uses it at 0.017 to 0.25 mm of approach on 0.07 to 1 mm2 of contact. No source gives hickory's pressure against depth at that scale
column3: unbounded; the same table row gives 12.1 MPa at the proportional limit of compression across the grain, which is a compression test and no bound on an indentation pressure
column4: the shaft strike's crush onset, peak force and contact time
column5: hickory indentation measured at sub-millimetre depth under a small-radius edge

column2: the hardness test is static (0.25 in/min in ASTM D143 as FPL notes quote it; the standard itself was not read) and the strike runs at 6 m/s, about 57,000 times faster. FPL-GTR-282 p. 5-38 gives about 10 % more strength for failure in 1 s than in about 5 min, and nothing near this rate. The law applies no rate correction
column3: unbounded; no hickory datum found. Spruce sapwood rose about 20 % across the grain from 8e-3 to 1000 1/s (Widehammar, read second hand)
column4: the shaft strike's crush onset, peak force and contact time
column5: dynamic compression or indentation of hickory across the grain near 1e4 1/s

column2: the crushing line, F = p A(d), is labelled Thornton (1997, J. Appl. Mech. 64, 383) in mean-pressure form. That paper is a theory for elastic-perfectly plastic spheres with a limit on the peak pressure, not a measurement on wood, and its full text was not read, so the equations in lib.rs Crush are not verified against it. A crushing cellular solid loses volume, which a perfectly plastic sphere does not
column4: the shape of the loading curve
column5: read the paper; a measured force-depth curve of hickory under an edge

column2: the law uses the Hertz area, half the edge's truncation of the shaft. The projected area a hardness test divides by at half embedment is the ball's full truncation. No source says which one applies to crushing hickory; the code takes the lower
column3: a factor of 2 in area, and in force at a given depth
column4: the crush force at a given depth
column5: contact area measured on crushed hickory

column2: the permanent set, s = d_m - sqrt(d_m d_y), 184 um of a 248 um approach at 6 m/s (74 %), comes from the construction in lib.rs Crush, not from a measurement on wood. FPL-GTR-282 Chapter 5 gives no unloading or recovery data across the grain
column4: the rebound, so the contact time and the energy left in the wood
column5: loading and unloading curves of hickory across the grain

column2: the unloading stiffness, K (d_m/d_y)^(1/4), 1.96 K at 6 m/s, applies Hertz's law with the undamaged elastic constants to crushed wood; nothing measured
column5: loading and unloading curves of hickory across the grain

column2: a crash is normally played glancing with the shoulder of the stick. Both strikes here are purely normal: the tip strike the site plays and the shaft strike, which has no friction or motion along the edge. Tangential contact is not modelled
column4: comparing either strike with a played crash
column5: a tangential contact owner, once the crush law is settled (ruling 9525)
